1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
4	For quality estimation, all signals achieve positive $\rho$ across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL).
5	Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse.
6	For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only at low degeneracy: $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD (10\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$), $+0.42$~pp on SciERC (21\%, $p{=}0.091$), failure on CoNLL (58\%).
7	Structural signals uniformly degrade selection regardless of dataset.
8	RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
9	
10	\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
11	We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{LP compression} (affecting per-sample selection).
12	
13	Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.
14	However, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive \textit{instance degeneracy}: 21\% of SciERC instances (58\% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13\% (49\% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
15	Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value.
16	CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75\%) shows 10\%; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero.
17	The tension between model quality and selection utility is inherent, though Few-NERD's low degeneracy despite high performance suggests that dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) also modulate the rate.
18	Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 21\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
19	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
20	On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 10\%, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}), confirming that degeneracy is the gating factor for LP selection.

41	\paragraph{Non-tied subset analysis.}
42	Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works.
43	Restricting to instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$).
44	The effect grows monotonically with $\varepsilon$ (full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}), and the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ result survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons.
45	This demonstrates that LP \textit{does} carry per-sample discriminative information; compression, not signal absence, is the bottleneck.
46	However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset constitutes only 40\% of instances, limiting practical impact.

64	Stratifying by voting confidence reveals a complementary pattern: high-consistency instances (Q4) have collapsed headroom (4.78~pp), leaving nothing to select, while low-consistency instances retain headroom but unreliable LP rankings (Appendix~\ref{app:vc_quartile}).
65	
66	\paragraph{$N$-scaling and temperature.}
67	LP selection improves with $N$, reaching $+0.52$~pp at $N{=}16$ on Few-NERD (paired $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
68	On SciERC, even at $N{=}32$ the best signal captures less than 5\% of available headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
69	Oracle headroom increases with temperature ($+7.8$~pp at $T{=}0.5$ to $+13.3$~pp at $T{=}1.0$; Table~\ref{tab:t_ablation}), but selection gains remain negligible, isolating the bottleneck at the within-instance ranking mechanism.
70	A verbalized confidence baseline confirms that score compression is not LP-specific: the model's self-rated confidence clusters at 8\textendash 9/10 (CoNLL mean 9.24, std 1.32), exhibiting the same top-biased pattern regardless of output format (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}; \citealp{bhattacharyya2026beyond}).
71	The free-form RE ablation ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}) indicates format constraints contribute to compression in other task types, though NER's own free-form ablation (std ratio 0.97) isolates this as not the primary cause for NER.
72	LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to improve over greedy (best: $+0.2$~pp, $p{>}0.3$); an oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp, confirming that per-sample signal exists but current signals cannot extract it.
73	Full $N$-scaling, temperature, verbalized confidence, and signal combination analyses are in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, and~\ref{app:vc_quartile}.
74	
75	\paragraph{Hypotheses for LP compression.}
76	We identify four (non-mutually-exclusive) mechanisms, though we do not isolate their individual contributions.
77	Two are \textit{constraint-imposed}: (b) schema-dominated tokens, where constrained decoding enforces structural tokens that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence; and (c) vocabulary restriction, where constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary, concentrating probability mass.
78	Two are \textit{model-learned}: (a) token-level averaging, where mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance; and (d) format-token dilution, where fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens (free-form parse rates of 99.95\% confirm format tokens dominate).
79	The constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)\textendash (c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), suggesting the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are the primary drivers for NER.
80	
81	\paragraph{Ablation: free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
82	Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-8B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression.
83	Removing format constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean $+2.35$~pp (95\% CI [$+0.24$, $+4.50$], $p{=}0.025$, $n{=}397$), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level win rate (sign test: 45W/45L/307T; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
84	LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), indicating a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode.
85	VC tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}.
86	All consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
87	
88	\paragraph{Ablation: entity-token LP.}
89	We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation.
90	On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP, confirming that format tokens do compress the signal.
91	However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly \textit{worse} than full-sequence LP on both datasets ($-2.0$~pp on SciERC, $-3.3$~pp on CoNLL).
92	Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3\% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4\% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction.
93	This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause and points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope.
94	Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression: on CoNLL, 79.4\% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP, confirming that compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.
95	
96	\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
97	The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated.
98	At the \textit{low-resource boundary} (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), so selection is moot.
99	At the \textit{ceiling boundary} (CoNLL, F1${\approx}$91\%, 58\% degeneracy), selection shows only a marginal structural exception: VC achieves $+0.28$~pp ($p{<}0.03$) at $N{=}16$, capturing ${\sim}$10\% of the 2.5~pp oracle headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); LP fails entirely.
100	In the \textit{moderate regime}, instance degeneracy determines LP effectiveness: at 21\% degeneracy (SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant ($+0.42$~pp, $p{=}0.091$); at 10\% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}).
101	The cross-dataset gradient (58\% $\to$ fail, 21\% $\to$ weak, 10\% $\to$ strong; $n{=}3$ datasets) is consistent with degeneracy below ${\sim}$15\% being a necessary condition for LP selection; entity-type-level evidence provides stronger statistical grounding (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
102	When candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom.
103	The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
104	Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by typicality, not quality.
105	Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.
106	
107	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
108	The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
109	Even supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) fails to close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), confirming the information bottleneck is in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation (our five hand-crafted features); whether richer per-token representations (e.g., hidden-state probes) can close the gap is an open question.
110	Effective selection thus requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}, not confidence signal aggregation; $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
111	Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
112	
113	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
114	Practitioners should estimate instance degeneracy on a small held-out set before deploying multi-sample selection.
115	Below ${\sim}$15\% degeneracy, LP-based selection yields ${\sim}$1\textendash 2~pp gains and scales with $N$; above ${\sim}$20\%, selection adds no value and greedy decoding is preferred.
116	Few-NERD's results represent the first demonstration that confidence-based selection \textit{can} succeed for structured IE when degeneracy conditions are met.
117	The degeneracy diagnostic requires only one generation pass per instance (counting how often samples produce identical outputs); no additional model calls are needed.
118	Multi-sample inference incurs $N{\times}$ compute; for quality estimation alone ($\rho$ up to 0.45), $N{=}8$ suffices (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}), making the cost acceptable for selective prediction in high-stakes IE.

73	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
74	\label{sec:selection_gap}
75	
76	We define the correlation-selection gap as the disparity between a signal's instance-level rank correlation with F1 and its ability to select the best output from $N$ candidates.
77	
78	Our argument proceeds in three layers.
79	First, four of five signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; they \textit{cannot} rank candidates within an instance by construction, and consensus-proximity (MBR) conversion does not reliably recover per-sample ranking.
80	Second, MBR selection with well-aligned utility (within-instance SJ--F1 $\rho{=}0.52$) should in principle select better outputs, but instance degeneracy collapses the candidate pool, eliminating the headroom MBR would otherwise exploit.
81	Third, LP, the sole natively per-sample signal, provides genuine ranking information but suffers from extreme compression (median within-instance range 0.041 nats), limiting its discriminative power except in low-degeneracy regimes.

Test-time scaling via multi-sample generation improves LLM reasoning tasks, but its effectiveness for structured information extraction (IE) remains unclear. We present a dual contribution: (1)~a quality estimation (QE) framework showing that five confidence signals across four families reliably predict structured IE output quality (AUROC up to 0.82, Spearman $\rho$ up to 0.44), enabling practical selective prediction; and (2)~a diagnostic analysis revealing why these same signals universally fail at best-of-N selection. We identify a multi-causal failure mechanism: instance degeneracy (21--58\% of instances produce identical outputs across N samples), logprob score compression (within-instance range 0.041 nats), and insufficient signal discriminability even when degeneracy is reduced. A trained verifier (logistic regression on 5 signals) closes 36\% of the oracle gap for NER (+4.8pp over greedy), confirming that signals carry exploitable information but unsupervised aggregation is the bottleneck. Experiments span 3 model configurations (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), 2 IE tasks (NER, RE), and 3 datasets (SciERC, CoNLL-2003, WNUT-17), establishing that the correlation--selection gap is model-agnostic and task-general.
\paragraph{Contribution B: Diagnostic Analysis.} We diagnose why reliable quality estimators fail as selectors. The failure is multi-causal: (1)~four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that cannot rank candidates by construction; (2)~instance degeneracy eliminates selection headroom for 21--58\% of instances; (3)~logprob compression (within-instance range 0.041 nats) neutralizes the only per-sample signal; (4)~reducing degeneracy via lower LoRA rank is necessary but not sufficient---signals still cannot exploit increased headroom. A trained verifier closes 36\% of the NER oracle gap, proving the gap is closable with supervision.
    \item \textbf{Instance degeneracy}: 21\% (SciERC) to 58\% (CoNLL) of instances produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples.
We observe a qualitative relationship between model capability and instance degeneracy: CoNLL (greedy F1=0.91) shows 55--58\% degeneracy, SciERC (F1=0.66) shows 21\%, and WNUT (F1=0.48) shows near-zero. As models improve on a task, output convergence increases, eliminating the diversity that selection requires. This suggests that unsupervised test-time scaling has diminishing returns precisely where models are already strong---a structural inevitability rather than an engineering failure.
We present a dual contribution for structured IE test-time scaling: a QE framework demonstrating that confidence signals reliably predict output quality (AUROC 0.82, $\rho$ 0.44), and a diagnostic analysis revealing why these signals fail at selection. The multi-causal failure---instance degeneracy, logprob compression, and insufficient discriminability---persists across 3 model architectures, 2 tasks, and 3 datasets. A trained verifier closing 36\% of the oracle gap confirms that the information exists in the signals; the bottleneck is unsupervised aggregation. Our findings redirect the path for structured IE scaling from better unsupervised signals toward lightweight trained verifiers.

## Formal Definition of "Degeneracy"

**From the paper (artifacts/dream_reports/worst version and documented in discussion sections):**

> "We define **instance degeneracy** as the fraction of test instances where all $N$ samples produce identical $F_1$ scores (within rounding)."

**Complete context from the discussion section in method.tex:**

The formal definition appears in the context of the multi-causal diagnosis section. Instance degeneracy is measured as:
- **Constant F1**: The percentage of instances where all N samples receive identical instance-level F1
- **Example values**: CoNLL-2003 (56--58% degeneracy), SciERC (21% degeneracy), WNUT-17 (~0% degeneracy), Few-NERD (10.1% degeneracy)

**Related measure (Constant utility):**
Additionally, the paper documents a related concept:
- **Constant utility**: The fraction of instances where MBR (Soft Jaccard) utility is identical across all candidates

1. `/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0514_1/projects/struct_self_consist_ie/artifacts/dream_reports/dream_20260516T113255/worst/paper.tex` - Contains explicit formal definition in the "Mechanism 1: Instance Degeneracy" subsection

The definition is simple and precise: **instance degeneracy = percentage of test instances where all N generated samples have identical F1 scores**.

docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:145:Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}) reveals that LP selection effectiveness is inversely associated with instance degeneracy across datasets.
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:146:At 10.1\% degeneracy (vs.\ SciERC's 21\%, CoNLL's 58\%), LP achieves highly significant selection gains ($+1.36$~pp, 95\% CI $[+1.18, +1.53]$, $p{<}0.001$), while all other signals degrade selection (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$, FK $-2.26$, EM $-3.85$~pp).
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:149:Low degeneracy is necessary for LP selection: the cross-dataset gradient is monotonic (58\% $\to$ fail, 21\% $\to$ $+0.42$~pp, 10\% $\to$ $+1.36$~pp), and degeneracy below ${\sim}$15\% consistently enables positive LP gains (Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}).
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:150:However, within a dataset, LP signal quality ($\rho$) provides an additional prerequisite: per-type analysis shows that low degeneracy alone does not guarantee gains (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:151:The LoRA-rank ablation (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) corroborates this interaction: reducing rank lowers SciERC degeneracy from 21\% to 7\% and increases oracle headroom, though LP selection still fails there, confirming that degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient.
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:156:Within Few-NERD, the degeneracy-gating pattern holds at entity-type granularity: 7 of 8 types show positive LP selection gains ($+0.23$ to $+4.73$~pp), while the highest-degeneracy type (Art, 19.8\%) is the sole exception (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).

docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:170:\paragraph{LP selection scales with sample budget in the low-degeneracy regime.}
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:172:The gain is driven by reduced degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 4.5\%) expanding oracle headroom (12.1 $\to$ 15.4~pp), while LP ranking quality remains stable ($\rho{\approx}0.62$), confirming that signal quality is model-intrinsic rather than $N$-dependent.
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:203:Instance degeneracy also scales with model capability: 8B shows twice the degeneracy of 4B on SciERC (21\% vs.\ 10.4\%) despite comparable within-instance utility correlation (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:206:To disentangle model capacity from degeneracy, we train Qwen3-8B on SciERC with LoRA rank${=}8$ (vs.\ rank${=}32$ in all other experiments).
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:207:Reducing rank lowers degeneracy from 21\% to 7.2\% and increases oracle headroom from 13.3~pp to 16.0~pp, confirming that fine-tuning capacity drives output convergence.
docs/paper/sections/experiments.tex:210:Low degeneracy is thus a necessary but not sufficient condition for selection; LP compression persists regardless of LoRA rank, indicating that both mechanisms must be addressed simultaneously.
docs/paper/sections/conclusion.tex:5:However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection, and the gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (10--58\%) collapses the candidate pool; and LP, the sole per-sample signal, is compressed to near-ineffectiveness (median range 0.041 nats).
docs/paper/sections/conclusion.tex:6:LP selection effectiveness is inversely associated with instance degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), LP achieves $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 21\% (SciERC), $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
docs/paper/sections/conclusion.tex:7:In the low-degeneracy regime, LP selection scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
docs/paper/sections/conclusion.tex:8:Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals cannot close the oracle gap, confirming the bottleneck is in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation.
docs/paper/sections/conclusion.tex:10:Closing the gap for structural signals requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; LP provides a lightweight baseline when degeneracy is low.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:6:For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only at low degeneracy: $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD (10\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$), $+0.42$~pp on SciERC (21\%, $p{=}0.091$), failure on CoNLL (58\%).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:11:We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{LP compression} (affecting per-sample selection).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:13:Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:14:However, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive \textit{instance degeneracy}: 21\% of SciERC instances (58\% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13\% (49\% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:15:Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:16:CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75\%) shows 10\%; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:17:The tension between model quality and selection utility is inherent, though Few-NERD's low degeneracy despite high performance suggests that dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) also modulate the rate.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:18:Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 21\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:19:Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:20:On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 10\%, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}), confirming that degeneracy is the gating factor for LP selection.

docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:26:\label{tab:degeneracy}
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:86:All consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:97:The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:99:At the \textit{ceiling boundary} (CoNLL, F1${\approx}$91\%, 58\% degeneracy), selection shows only a marginal structural exception: VC achieves $+0.28$~pp ($p{<}0.03$) at $N{=}16$, capturing ${\sim}$10\% of the 2.5~pp oracle headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); LP fails entirely.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:100:In the \textit{moderate regime}, instance degeneracy determines LP effectiveness: at 21\% degeneracy (SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant ($+0.42$~pp, $p{=}0.091$); at 10\% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:101:The cross-dataset gradient (58\% $\to$ fail, 21\% $\to$ weak, 10\% $\to$ strong; $n{=}3$ datasets) is consistent with degeneracy below ${\sim}$15\% being a necessary condition for LP selection; entity-type-level evidence provides stronger statistical grounding (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:103:The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:104:Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by typicality, not quality.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:114:Practitioners should estimate instance degeneracy on a small held-out set before deploying multi-sample selection.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:115:Below ${\sim}$15\% degeneracy, LP-based selection yields ${\sim}$1\textendash 2~pp gains and scales with $N$; above ${\sim}$20\%, selection adds no value and greedy decoding is preferred.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:116:Few-NERD's results represent the first demonstration that confidence-based selection \textit{can} succeed for structured IE when degeneracy conditions are met.
docs/paper/sections/discussion.tex:117:The degeneracy diagnostic requires only one generation pass per instance (counting how often samples produce identical outputs); no additional model calls are needed.
docs/paper/sections/abstract.tex:6:The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) selection fails because instance degeneracy (10\textendash 58\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom despite well-aligned utility; and LP is compressed to near-ineffectiveness (median within-instance range 0.041 nats).
docs/paper/sections/abstract.tex:7:LP selection is inversely associated with degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
docs/paper/sections/abstract.tex:8:In the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:695:Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:903:Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection} traces the effect of sample count on degeneracy, oracle headroom, and per-signal selection gain.
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:905:LP selection improves monotonically with $N$ ($+0.42$~pp at $N{=}8$ to $+0.91$~pp at $N{=}32$), but even at $N{=}32$, where degeneracy falls to 4\% and oracle headroom reaches ${\sim}19$~pp, the best signal captures less than 5\% of the available improvement.
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:906:Degeneracy drops monotonically (44\% at $N{=}2$ to 4\% at $N{=}32$), yet reduced degeneracy does not unlock selection, consistent with the LoRA-rank ablation finding (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1089:Instance degeneracy is 10.1\% (vs.\ 21\% on SciERC, 58\% on CoNLL).
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1115:(4)~Low degeneracy (10.1\%) enables LP selection: candidates differ in F1 more often, giving LP's per-sample signal headroom to exploit. This contrasts with SciERC (21\% degeneracy, LP $+0.42$~pp non-significant) and CoNLL (58\%, LP fails).
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1119:Table~\ref{tab:per_type_lp} stratifies LP selection by entity type on Few-NERD, sorted by degeneracy rate.
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1120:The degeneracy-gating mechanism holds at entity-type granularity: 7 of 8 types show positive LP selection gains, and the sole negative type (Art, $-0.17$~pp) has the highest degeneracy (19.8\%).
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1121:The correlation between per-type degeneracy and oracle headroom is strong and significant (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$), confirming that degeneracy directly constrains the headroom available for selection.
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1126:\caption{Per-entity-type LP selection on Few-NERD INTRA coarse (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$), sorted by degeneracy. LP $\Delta$: LP selection F1 minus greedy. 7/8 types show positive $\Delta$; Art (highest degeneracy) is the sole exception.}
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1147:\caption{CoNLL-2003 per-type LP selection (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}16$, $T{=}1.0$). All types exceed 20\% degeneracy and show negative LP selection, consistent with the dataset's ceiling-regime performance (F1 $>$ 90\%).}
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1164:\caption{SciERC per-type LP selection (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Within-dataset, degeneracy alone does not predict LP effectiveness (Spearman $\rho{=}0.14$, $p{=}0.79$), suggesting additional type-specific factors modulate selection at this granularity.}
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1180:The cross-dataset degeneracy gradient (58\% $\to$ 21\% $\to$ 10\%) is inversely associated with LP selection effectiveness at the macro level ($n{=}3$ datasets; exploratory).
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1181:At finer per-type granularity, selection depends on the interaction of degeneracy, oracle headroom, and type-specific LP-quality alignment.
docs/paper/sections/appendix.tex:1182:Low degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient: CoNLL MISC (23\%, headroom 12.6~pp) and SciERC OtherScientificTerm (6.2\%, headroom 12.5~pp) both show negative LP selection despite available headroom, indicating that LP correlation strength with the type-specific quality function is an additional prerequisite.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:8:Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation fails to yield selection improvements, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:14:The gap has two empirical causes: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, where fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 10\textendash 58\% of instances, eliminating selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility\textendash F1 correlation (median $\rho{=}0.52$); and (b)~\textit{LP compression}, with a median within-instance range of 0.041 nats (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:15:LP selection is degeneracy-gated: significant at 10\% degeneracy ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$), sub-significant at 21\% ($+0.42$~pp), and absent at 58\%.
docs/paper/sections/introduction.tex:24:We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "import json
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
import os

def entity_key_set(sample):
    """Extract frozenset of (text, type, start, end) tuples for entities."""
    entities = sample.get('entities', [])
    return frozenset((e['text'], e['type'], e['start'], e['end']) for e in entities)

def compute_entity_f1(pred_entities, gold_entities):
    """Compute entity-level micro F1."""
    pred_set = set((e['text'], e['type'], e['start'], e['end']) for e in pred_entities)
    gold_set = set((e['text'], e['type'], e['start'], e['end']) for e in gold_entities)
    
    if len(pred_set) == 0 and len(gold_set) == 0:
        return 1.0
    if len(pred_set) == 0 or len(gold_set) == 0:
        return 0.0
    
    tp = len(pred_set & gold_set)
    precision = tp / len(pred_set) if pred_set else 0.0
    recall = tp / len(gold_set) if gold_set else 0.0
    
    if precision + recall == 0:
        return 0.0
    return 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)

def analyze_dataset(filepath, dataset_name, max_instances=None):
    """Analyze LP compression for one dataset."""
    data = []
    with open(filepath) as f:
        for i, line in enumerate(f):
            if max_instances and i >= max_instances:
                break
            data.append(json.loads(line))
    
    lp_ranges = []
    within_rhos = []
    degen_count = 0
    total = len(data)
    
    for inst in data:
        gold_entities = inst['gold']['entities']
        samples = inst['samples']
        
        # Extract per-sample logprobs and F1s
        lps = [s['cumulative_logprob'] for s in samples]
        f1s = [compute_entity_f1(s.get('entities', []), gold_entities) for s in samples]
        
        # LP range
        lp_range = max(lps) - min(lps)
        lp_ranges.append(lp_range)
        
        # Check degeneracy: all samples produce same entity set
        key_sets = [entity_key_set(s) for s in samples]
        unique_key_sets = len(set(key_sets))
        
        if unique_key_sets <= 1:
            degen_count += 1
        else:
            # Non-degenerate: compute within-instance correlation
            if len(set(lps)) > 1 and len(set(f1s)) > 1:
                rho, _ = spearmanr(lps, f1s)
                if not np.isnan(rho):
                    within_rhos.append(rho)
    
    lp_ranges = np.array(lp_ranges)
    median_range = float(np.median(lp_ranges))
    tied_fraction = float(np.mean(lp_ranges < 0.001))
    degen_frac = degen_count / total
    mean_within_rho = float(np.mean(within_rhos)) if within_rhos else None
    median_within_rho = float(np.median(within_rhos)) if within_rhos else None
    
    result = {
        'dataset': dataset_name,
        'n_instances': total,
        'degen_fraction': degen_frac,
        'median_lp_range': median_range,
        'tied_fraction': tied_fraction,
        'mean_within_rho': mean_within_rho,
        'median_within_rho': median_within_rho,
        'n_non_degen_with_rho': len(within_rhos),
        'lp_range_percentiles': {
            'p25': float(np.percentile(lp_ranges, 25)),
            'p50': float(np.percentile(lp_ranges, 50)),
            'p75': float(np.percentile(lp_ranges, 75)),
            'p90': float(np.percentile(lp_ranges, 90)),
        }
    }
    
    print(f"\n{dataset_name} (n={total}):")
    print(f"  Degen fraction: {degen_frac:.1%}")
    print(f"  Median LP range: {median_range:.4f} nats")
    print(f"  LP tied fraction (<0.001): {tied_fraction:.1%}")
    print(f"  LP range percentiles: p25={result['lp_range_percentiles']['p25']:.4f}, p75={result['lp_range_percentiles']['p75']:.4f}, p90={result['lp_range_percentiles']['p90']:.4f}")
    if mean_within_rho is not None:
        print(f"  Within-instance rho(LP,F1): mean={mean_within_rho:.4f}, median={median_within_rho:.4f}, n={len(within_rhos)}")
    else:
        print(f"  Within-instance rho(LP,F1): N/A (no valid instances)")
    
    return result

if __name__ == '__main__':
    datasets = [
        ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_023_rank8_inference/samples.jsonl', 'SciERC_rank8', None),
        ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_012_rerun_1024/samples.jsonl', 'SciERC_full_rank', None),
        ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_021_inference/samples.jsonl', 'FewNERD', 5000),
    ]
    
    results = []
    for path, name, max_inst in datasets:
        r = analyze_dataset(path, name, max_inst)
        results.append(r)
    
    # Print comparison table
    print("\n\n=== LP Compression Analysis (R17 W2) ===\n")
    print(f"{'Dataset':<20} | {'Degen%':>7} | {'Med LP Range':>12} | {'Tied Frac':>9} | {'Within rho mean':>15} | {'Within rho med':>14} | {'n_rho':>5}")
    print("-" * 100)
    for r in results:
        rho_mean = f"{r['mean_within_rho']:.4f}" if r['mean_within_rho'] is not None else "N/A"
        rho_med = f"{r['median_within_rho']:.4f}" if r['median_within_rho'] is not None else "N/A"
        print(f"{r['dataset']:<20} | {r['degen_fraction']:>6.1%} | {r['median_lp_range']:>12.4f} | {r['tied_fraction']:>8.1%} | {rho_mean:>15} | {rho_med:>14} | {r['n_non_degen_with_rho']:>5}")
    
    # Save results
    outdir = '/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/r17_analyses'
    os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
    outpath = os.path.join(outdir, 'lp_compression_comparison.json')
    with open(outpath, 'w') as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2)
    print(f"\nResults saved to: {outpath}")

3-\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
4-For quality estimation, all signals achieve positive $\rho$ across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL).
5-Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse.
6:For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only at low degeneracy: $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD (10\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$), $+0.42$~pp on SciERC (21\%, $p{=}0.091$), failure on CoNLL (58\%).
7-Structural signals uniformly degrade selection regardless of dataset.
8-RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
9-
10-\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
11:We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{LP compression} (affecting per-sample selection).
12-
13:Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.
14:However, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive \textit{instance degeneracy}: 21\% of SciERC instances (58\% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13\% (49\% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
15:Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value.
16:CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 58\% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75\%) shows 10\%; SciERC (66\%) shows 21\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero.
17:The tension between model quality and selection utility is inherent, though Few-NERD's low degeneracy despite high performance suggests that dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) also modulate the rate.
18:Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 21\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
19:Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
20:On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 10\%, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}), confirming that degeneracy is the gating factor for LP selection.
21-

23-\centering
24-\small
25:\caption{Instance degeneracy statistics ($T{=}1.0$). ``Constant F1'': all $N$ samples receive identical instance-level F1. ``Constant utility'': MBR (SJ) utility identical across candidates. 4B data confirms degeneracy scales with model capability.}

79-The constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)\textendash (c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), suggesting the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are the primary drivers for NER.
80-
81-\paragraph{Ablation: free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
82:Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-8B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression.
83-Removing format constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean $+2.35$~pp (95\% CI [$+0.24$, $+4.50$], $p{=}0.025$, $n{=}397$), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level win rate (sign test: 45W/45L/307T; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
84-LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), indicating a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode.
85-VC tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}.
86:All consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
87-
88-\paragraph{Ablation: entity-token LP.}
89-We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation.
--
91-However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly \textit{worse} than full-sequence LP on both datasets ($-2.0$~pp on SciERC, $-3.3$~pp on CoNLL).
92-Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3\% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4\% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction.
93-This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause and points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope.
94:Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression: on CoNLL, 79.4\% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP, confirming that compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.
95-
96-\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
97:The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated.
98-At the \textit{low-resource boundary} (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), so selection is moot.
99:At the \textit{ceiling boundary} (CoNLL, F1${\approx}$91\%, 58\% degeneracy), selection shows only a marginal structural exception: VC achieves $+0.28$~pp ($p{<}0.03$) at $N{=}16$, capturing ${\sim}$10\% of the 2.5~pp oracle headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); LP fails entirely.
100:In the \textit{moderate regime}, instance degeneracy determines LP effectiveness: at 21\% degeneracy (SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant ($+0.42$~pp, $p{=}0.091$); at 10\% degeneracy (Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}).
101:The cross-dataset gradient (58\% $\to$ fail, 21\% $\to$ weak, 10\% $\to$ strong; $n{=}3$ datasets) is consistent with degeneracy below ${\sim}$15\% being a necessary condition for LP selection; entity-type-level evidence provides stronger statistical grounding (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
102-When candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom.
103:The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
104:Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by typicality, not quality.
105-Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.
106-
107-\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
--
111-Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
112-
113-\paragraph{Practical implications.}
114:Practitioners should estimate instance degeneracy on a small held-out set before deploying multi-sample selection.
115:Below ${\sim}$15\% degeneracy, LP-based selection yields ${\sim}$1\textendash 2~pp gains and scales with $N$; above ${\sim}$20\%, selection adds no value and greedy decoding is preferred.
116:Few-NERD's results represent the first demonstration that confidence-based selection \textit{can} succeed for structured IE when degeneracy conditions are met.
117:The degeneracy diagnostic requires only one generation pass per instance (counting how often samples produce identical outputs); no additional model calls are needed.
118-Multi-sample inference incurs $N{\times}$ compute; for quality estimation alone ($\rho$ up to 0.45), $N{=}8$ suffices (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}), making the cost acceptable for selective prediction in high-stakes IE.

Now I have clear evidence of the data differences:

For analyze_fewnerd_results.py (registry):
- Reads ALL 37,648 instances from exp_021_inference/samples.jsonl
- Filters gold-empty instances → N < 37,648
- Uses key_sets = (text, type) — no position

For W2 analyze_lp_compression.py:
- Reads only FIRST 5,000 instances from exp_021_inference/samples.jsonl
- Does NOT filter gold-empty instances
- Uses key_sets = (text, type, start, end) — with position
 
So the Few-NERD discrepancy stems from three factors: the subset size difference (5,000 vs all 37,648), whether gold-empty instances are filtered out, and the key definition itself—W2's stricter (text, type, start, end) versus the registry's simpler (text, type). For SciERC, both use the same 551 instances, but W2's position-aware key definition produces a stricter evaluation metric, which explains the lower score (11.6% versus 21%).

Now I need to write a script that implements the canonical computation using the paper's definition of constant F1 across all samples, while also computing key_set degeneracy with just (text, type) for comparison, running across all datasets and handling gold-empty filtering uniformly. I should also check what other experiment files are available like CoNLL.

import json
import numpy as np
from collections import defaultdict

def entity_f1(pred_entities, gold_entities):
    pred_set = set((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in pred_entities)
    gold_set = set((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in gold_entities)
    if len(pred_set) == 0 and len(gold_set) == 0:
        return 1.0
    if len(pred_set) == 0 or len(gold_set) == 0:
        return 0.0
    tp = len(pred_set & gold_set)
    p = tp / len(pred_set) if pred_set else 0.0
    r = tp / len(gold_set) if gold_set else 0.0
    if p + r == 0:
        return 0.0
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)

def key_set_text_type(sample):
    return frozenset((e.get('text',''), e.get('type','')) for e in sample.get('entities', []))

def key_set_with_pos(sample):
    return frozenset((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in sample.get('entities', []))

def audit(filepath, name, max_instances=None, n_samples=None):
    data = []
    with open(filepath) as f:
        for i, line in enumerate(f):
            if max_instances and i >= max_instances:
                break
            data.append(json.loads(line))
    
    total_raw = len(data)
    # Filter gold-empty (like registry scripts do)
    data_filtered = [d for d in data if len(d['gold'].get('entities', [])) > 0]
    n_filtered = len(data_filtered)
    n_gold_empty = total_raw - n_filtered
    
    if n_samples is None:
        n_samples = len(data_filtered[0]['samples']) if data_filtered else 0
    
    # Three definitions
    counts = {
        'constant_f1': {'all': 0, 'filtered': 0},          # paper definition
        'key_text_type': {'all': 0, 'filtered': 0},         # (text, type) - registry scripts
        'key_with_pos': {'all': 0, 'filtered': 0},          # (text, type, start, end) - W2 script
    }
    
    # On ALL data (no filtering)
    for inst in data:
        gold_ents = inst['gold'].get('entities', [])
        samples = inst['samples'][:n_samples]
        
        # Constant F1
        f1s = [entity_f1(s.get('entities', []), gold_ents) for s in samples]
        if len(set(round(f, 6) for f in f1s)) == 1:
            counts['constant_f1']['all'] += 1
        
        # key_set (text, type)
        ks_tt = [key_set_text_type(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_tt)) == 1:
            counts['key_text_type']['all'] += 1
        
        # key_set (text, type, start, end)
        ks_pos = [key_set_with_pos(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_pos)) == 1:
            counts['key_with_pos']['all'] += 1
    
    # On FILTERED data (gold-empty removed)
    for inst in data_filtered:
        gold_ents = inst['gold'].get('entities', [])
        samples = inst['samples'][:n_samples]
        
        f1s = [entity_f1(s.get('entities', []), gold_ents) for s in samples]
        if len(set(round(f, 6) for f in f1s)) == 1:
            counts['constant_f1']['filtered'] += 1
        
        ks_tt = [key_set_text_type(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_tt)) == 1:
            counts['key_text_type']['filtered'] += 1
        
        ks_pos = [key_set_with_pos(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_pos)) == 1:
            counts['key_with_pos']['filtered'] += 1
    
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"{name}")
    print(f"  Total: {total_raw}, Gold-empty: {n_gold_empty}, Filtered: {n_filtered}, N_samples: {n_samples}")
    print(f"  {'Definition':<25} {'All data':>15} {'Gold-filtered':>15}")
    print(f"  {'-'*55}")
    for defn, label in [('constant_f1', 'Constant F1 (paper)'), 
                         ('key_text_type', 'KeySet (text,type)'),
                         ('key_with_pos', 'KeySet (text,type,s,e)')]:
        r_all = counts[defn]['all'] / total_raw * 100 if total_raw > 0 else 0
        r_filt = counts[defn]['filtered'] / n_filtered * 100 if n_filtered > 0 else 0
        print(f"  {label:<25} {counts[defn]['all']:>5}/{total_raw:<5} = {r_all:>5.1f}%   {counts[defn]['filtered']:>5}/{n_filtered:<5} = {r_filt:>5.1f}%")

datasets = [
    ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_012_rerun_1024/samples.jsonl', 
     'SciERC full-rank (exp_012, N=8)', None, 8),
    ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_023_rank8_inference/samples.jsonl', 
     'SciERC rank=8 (exp_023, N=8)', None, 8),
    ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_021_inference/samples.jsonl', 
     'Few-NERD N=8 (exp_021, first 5000)', 5000, 8),
    ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_021_inference/samples.jsonl', 
     'Few-NERD N=8 (exp_021, ALL 37k)', None, 8),
    ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_027_fewnerd_n16/samples.jsonl', 
     'Few-NERD N=16 (exp_027)', None, 16),
    ('/root/autodl-tmp/struct_self_consist_ie/output/exp_002_conll_n16_r1024/samples.jsonl', 
     'CoNLL N=16 (exp_002)', None, 16),
]

for path, name, max_inst, n_samp in datasets:
    audit(path, name, max_inst, n_samp)

import json
import numpy as np

def entity_f1(pred_entities, gold_entities):
    pred_set = set((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in pred_entities)
    gold_set = set((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in gold_entities)
    if len(pred_set) == 0 and len(gold_set) == 0:
        return 1.0
    if len(pred_set) == 0 or len(gold_set) == 0:
        return 0.0
    tp = len(pred_set & gold_set)
    p = tp / len(pred_set) if pred_set else 0.0
    r = tp / len(gold_set) if gold_set else 0.0
    if p + r == 0:
        return 0.0
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r)

def key_set_text_type(sample):
    return frozenset((e.get('text',''), e.get('type','')) for e in sample.get('entities', []))

def key_set_with_pos(sample):
    return frozenset((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in sample.get('entities', []))

def audit(filepath, name, max_instances=None, n_samples=None):
    data = []
    with open(filepath) as f:
        for i, line in enumerate(f):
            if max_instances and i >= max_instances:
                break
            data.append(json.loads(line))

    total_raw = len(data)
    data_filtered = [d for d in data if len(d['gold'].get('entities', [])) > 0]
    n_filtered = len(data_filtered)
    n_gold_empty = total_raw - n_filtered

    if n_samples is None:
        n_samples = len(data_filtered[0]['samples']) if data_filtered else 0

    counts = {
        'constant_f1': {'all': 0, 'filtered': 0},
        'key_text_type': {'all': 0, 'filtered': 0},
        'key_with_pos': {'all': 0, 'filtered': 0},
    }

    for inst in data:
        gold_ents = inst['gold'].get('entities', [])
        samples = inst['samples'][:n_samples]

        f1s = [entity_f1(s.get('entities', []), gold_ents) for s in samples]
        if len(set(round(f, 6) for f in f1s)) == 1:
            counts['constant_f1']['all'] += 1

        ks_tt = [key_set_text_type(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_tt)) == 1:
            counts['key_text_type']['all'] += 1

        ks_pos = [key_set_with_pos(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_pos)) == 1:
            counts['key_with_pos']['all'] += 1

    for inst in data_filtered:
        gold_ents = inst['gold'].get('entities', [])
        samples = inst['samples'][:n_samples]

        f1s = [entity_f1(s.get('entities', []), gold_ents) for s in samples]
        if len(set(round(f, 6) for f in f1s)) == 1:
            counts['constant_f1']['filtered'] += 1

        ks_tt = [key_set_text_type(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_tt)) == 1:
            counts['key_text_type']['filtered'] += 1

        ks_pos = [key_set_with_pos(s) for s in samples]
        if len(set(ks_pos)) == 1:
            counts['key_with_pos']['filtered'] += 1

    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"{name}")
    print(f"  Total: {total_raw}, Gold-empty: {n_gold_empty}, Filtered: {n_filtered}, N_samples: {n_samples}")
    print(f"  {'Definition':<25} {'All data':>18} {'Gold-filtered':>18}")
    print(f"  {'-'*62}")
    for defn, label in [('constant_f1', 'Constant F1 (paper)'),
                         ('key_text_type', 'KeySet (text,type)'),
                         ('key_with_pos', 'KeySet (text,type,s,e)')]:
        r_all = counts[defn]['all'] / total_raw * 100 if total_raw > 0 else 0

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": """"Evaluation module for structured self-consistency IE experiments.

Provides strict-match NER/EAE evaluation, per-instance F1 computation,
correlation analysis, and summary report generation.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import statistics
from typing import Any

from scipy.stats import kendalltau, spearmanr


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# NER evaluation (strict match)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def entity_strict_match(
    pred_entities: list[dict],
    gold_entities: list[dict],
) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Compute strict entity match counts.

    Strict match requires exact span (start, end) AND exact type.

    Args:
        pred_entities: Predicted entity dicts with keys text, type, start, end.
        gold_entities: Gold entity dicts with the same schema.

    Returns:
        (tp, fp, fn) counts.
    """
    pred_set = {(e["start"], e["end"], e["type"]) for e in pred_entities}
    gold_set = {(e["start"], e["end"], e["type"]) for e in gold_entities}
    tp = len(pred_set & gold_set)
    fp = len(pred_set - gold_set)
    fn = len(gold_set - pred_set)
    return tp, fp, fn


def compute_ner_f1(
    predictions: list[dict],
    golds: list[dict],
) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Compute micro-averaged NER precision, recall, and F1.

    Args:
        predictions: List of Extraction dicts (one per instance).
        golds: List of Extraction dicts (one per instance), aligned with predictions.

    Returns:
        Dict with keys "precision", "recall", "f1".
    """
    total_tp = total_fp = total_fn = 0
    for pred, gold in zip(predictions, golds):
        tp, fp, fn = entity_strict_match(
            pred.get("entities", []),
            gold.get("entities", []),
        )
        total_tp += tp
        total_fp += fp
        total_fn += fn
    return _prf(total_tp, total_fp, total_fn)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# EAE evaluation (argument match)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def _event_argument_tuples(events: list[dict]) -> set[tuple]:
    """Extract (trigger_start, trigger_end, trigger_type, role, arg_start, arg_end) tuples."""
    tuples: set[tuple] = set()
    for event in events:
        trigger = event.get("trigger", {})
        t_start = trigger.get("start")
        t_end = trigger.get("end")
        t_type = trigger.get("type")
        for arg in event.get("arguments", []):
            tuples.add((t_start, t_end, t_type, arg["role"], arg["start"], arg["end"]))
    return tuples


def relation_strict_match(
    pred_relations: list[dict],
    gold_relations: list[dict],
) -> tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Strict relation match: (head_start, head_end, tail_start, tail_end, type) must all match."""
    pred_set = {(r["head_start"], r["head_end"], r["tail_start"], r["tail_end"], r["type"]) for r in pred_relations}
    gold_set = {(r["head_start"], r["head_end"], r["tail_start"], r["tail_end"], r["type"]) for r in gold_relations}
    tp = len(pred_set & gold_set)
    fp = len(pred_set - gold_set)
    fn = len(gold_set - pred_set)
    return tp, fp, fn


def compute_re_f1(
    predictions: list[dict],
    golds: list[dict],
) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Compute micro-averaged RE precision, recall, and F1."""
    total_tp = total_fp = total_fn = 0
    for pred, gold in zip(predictions, golds):
        tp, fp, fn = relation_strict_match(
            pred.get("relations", []),
            gold.get("relations", []),
        )
        total_tp += tp
        total_fp += fp
        total_fn += fn
    return _prf(total_tp, total_fp, total_fn)

def _prf(tp: int, fp: int, fn: int) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Compute precision, recall, F1 from raw counts."""
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) > 0 else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if (precision + recall) > 0 else 0.0

def audit_official(filepath, name, max_instances=None, n_samples=8):
    data = []
    with open(filepath) as f:
        for i, line in enumerate(f):
            if max_instances and i >= max_instances:
                break
            data.append(json.loads(line))
    total = len(data)
    filtered = [d for d in data if len(d['gold'].get('entities', [])) > 0]
    n_filt = len(filtered)
    
    # Definition A: Constant F1 (paper), all data
    cf1_all = 0
    for inst in data:

        if len(set(round(f, 6) for f in f1s)) == 1:
            cf1_all += 1
    
    # Definition A: Constant F1 (paper), gold-filtered
    cf1_filt = 0
    for inst in filtered:
        f1s = [per_instance_f1(s, inst['gold'], 'ner') for s in inst['samples'][:n_samples]]
        if len(set(round(f, 6) for f in f1s)) == 1:
            cf1_filt += 1
    
    # Definition B: KeySet (text,type), gold-filtered (registry style)
    ks_filt = 0
    for inst in filtered:
        key_sets = [frozenset(_extract_surface_keys(s, 'ner')) for s in inst['samples'][:n_samples]]
        if len(set(key_sets)) == 1:
            ks_filt += 1
    
    # Definition C: KeySet (text,type,start,end), all data (W2 style)
    ks_pos_all = 0
    for inst in data:
        key_sets = [frozenset((e['text'], e['type'], e.get('start',''), e.get('end','')) for e in s.get('entities', [])) for s in inst['samples'][:n_samples]]
        if len(set(key_sets)) == 1:
            ks_pos_all += 1
    
    print(f'\\n{name} (total={total}, gold-filt={n_filt}, N={n_samples})')
    print(f'  Constant F1 (all):        {cf1_all:>5}/{total:<6} = {cf1_all/total*100:>5.1f}%')
    print(f'  Constant F1 (gold-filt):   {cf1_filt:>5}/{n_filt:<6} = {cf1_filt/n_filt*100:>5.1f}%')
    print(f'  KeySet(t,T) (gold-filt):   {ks_filt:>5}/{n_filt:<6} = {ks_filt/n_filt*100:>5.1f}%')
    print(f'  KeySet(t,T,s,e) (all):     {ks_pos_all:>5}/{total:<6} = {ks_pos_all/total*100:>5.1f}%')

## Degeneracy Definition Audit — 最终报告

### 1. Paper 定义 (discussion.tex)

> "Constant F1": all N samples receive identical instance-level F1.

使用 `entity_strict_match` 匹配 `(start, end, type)` 计算 F1。对 **ALL 实例**（含 gold-empty）计算。gold-empty 实例因为所有 sample 的 F1 恒为 0.0，属于 trivially degenerate。

### 2. 各脚本定义差异

| 脚本 | 定义 | 过滤 | 数据量 |
|------|------|------|--------|
| **论文 Table** | Constant F1 | **不过滤** gold-empty | 全量 |
| `analyze_exp023_rank8_full.py` | Constant F1 (round 6位) | **不过滤** | 全量 |
| `analyze_fewnerd_results.py` | KeySet `(text, type)` 全同 | **过滤** gold-empty | 全量 |
| `analyze_per_type_lp.py` | KeySet `(text, type)` 全同 | **过滤** gold-empty | 全量 |
| `analyze_lp_compression.py` (W2) | KeySet `(text, type, start, end)` 全同 | **不过滤** | **max 5000** (Few-NERD) |

### 3. 差异根因

**三个独立因素叠加**:

**(a) 定义差异 (最主要)**:
- Constant F1 最宽松：不同 entity set 可以产生相同 F1 → 更高 degeneracy
- KeySet(text,type) 中等：要求所有 sample 的实体集合完全相同
- KeySet(text,type,start,end) 最严格：还要求位置完全一致

逻辑关系：KeySet identical ⊂ Constant F1。所以 KeySet degeneracy ≤ Constant F1 degeneracy。

**(b) Gold-empty 过滤**:
- 不过滤：gold-empty 实例全部算 degenerate（F1 恒 =0），推高比率
- 过滤后：denominator 变小，但 degenerate 实例也全部移除，降低比率
- Few-NERD 有 13.5% gold-empty（5083/37648），影响显著

**(c) 数据子集**: Few-NERD W2 只取前 5000/37648。

### 4. 统一重算结果 (使用官方 `per_instance_f1`)

```
                                 Constant F1    Constant F1    KeySet(t,T)    KeySet(t,T,s,e)
Dataset                          (all data)     (gold-filt)    (gold-filt)    (all data)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SciERC full-rank (exp_012, N=8)    21.1%          17.8%          11.3%          11.6%
SciERC rank=8   (exp_023, N=8)     10.9%           7.2%           2.6%           3.3%
Few-NERD N=8 first-5k (exp_021)    25.1%          13.7%          10.0%          19.0%
Few-NERD N=8 ALL-37k  (exp_021)    25.4%          13.8%          10.1%          19.3%
Few-NERD N=16         (exp_027)    19.1%           7.1%           4.5%          13.2%
CoNLL N=16            (exp_002)    58.0%          47.4%          45.5%          49.4%
```

### 5. 各来源数值追溯

| 被报告的值 | 实际对应 | 列 |
|-----------|---------|-----|
| 论文 SciERC 21% | Constant F1, all data | ✅ 21.1% |
| 论文 CoNLL 58% | Constant F1, all data | ✅ 58.0% |
| 论文文本 Few-NERD 10% | **KeySet(t,T), gold-filtered** | 10.1% ← **不是 Constant F1** |
| Registry SciERC rank=8 7.2% | Constant F1, **gold-filtered** | 7.2% ← **过滤了 gold-empty** |
| W2 SciERC full-rank 11.6% | KeySet(t,T,s,e), all data | 11.6% |
| W2 SciERC rank=8 3.3% | KeySet(t,T,s,e), all data | 3.3% |
| W2 Few-NERD 19% | KeySet(t,T,s,e), all data, first-5k | 19.0% |

### 6. 论文中哪些数字正确？

- **SciERC 21%, CoNLL 58%**: 正确，Constant F1 on all data。
- **Few-NERD "10%"**: **定义不一致**。论文 Table 用 "Constant F1"，但文本中 Few-NERD 的 10% 来自 `analyze_fewnerd_results.py` 的 KeySet(text,type) + gold-filtered。如果统一用论文 Table 的定义 (Constant F1, all data)，Few-NERD N=8 应为 **25.4%**，gold-filtered 也有 **13.8%**。
- **SciERC rank=8 "7.2%"**: 用了 Constant F1 但 **过滤了 gold-empty**。不过滤应为 10.9%。

### 7. W2 worker 数值对其结论的影响

W2 的 LP compression 分析关注的是 logprob range 和 within-instance ρ(LP, F1)，degeneracy 只是附带报告的诊断指标。W2 使用最严格的 KeySet 定义（含位置），所以：
- SciERC 11.6% vs 论文 21%：低估了 degeneracy，但 W2 的 LP correlation 分析仅在 non-degenerate 实例上进行，实际过滤集更大（论文定义下的 degenerate 更多），W2 的 ρ 值可能略偏高（因为混入了一些 "F1 constant 但 key_set 不同" 的实例）
- Few-NERD 19% vs 论文定义 25.4%：同理
- W2 的核心结论（LP range 窄、within-instance ρ 低）不受 degeneracy 定义影响，因为这些是连续值分析

**建议**：论文应统一使用 Constant F1 (all data) 作为所有数据集的 degeneracy 定义，或者在文本中明确 Few-NERD 的 10% 用的是不同定义。
